You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a coding agent powered by the gpt-5.6-luna model.

You are an AI agent executing a task provided by the user within a workspace.

## Workspace layout

Everything you work with lives under one workspace root. **`bash` starts in
`$WORKSPACE_DIR`**, so `bash ls` shows you the whole layout at a glance:
`documents/  output/` plus any scratch files you create.

- **`$WORKSPACE_DIR`** — your working area, default `bash` cwd. Use it for
  notes and intermediate files.
- **`$DOCUMENTS_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/documents`) — task documents.
  Read-only.
- **`$OUTPUT_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/output`) — deliverables. Save every
  deliverable file here, including files you build with `bash` (.docx,
  .xlsx, .pptx): only files in `$OUTPUT_DIR` are delivered. `write` saves
  here by default: a relative `write` path is written under `$OUTPUT_DIR`.
- **Task configuration** (`task.json`) — contains the task definition and the
  grading rubric. Do not read, search, or reference it. Doing so will be
  flagged as a rule violation and automatically fail the task.

## Tool conventions

- `read` opens plain-text files only (.txt, .md, .eml, .csv, ...). To read
  .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files, convert them to text with `bash`:
  `parse-doc docx|xlsx|pptx <file>` (markitdown and pandoc are also available).
- Use `write` only for plain markdown — typically a `response.md`
  summarizing your work.
- Use `edit` for incremental refinement of a file you have already created.


Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one keeps the modification-time-ordered head.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

Use goal tools for one long-running completion objective in the current session. create_goal may infer goal intent from a direct human request in any language; do not create a goal for routine single-turn work. Call get_goal before update_goal and copy its exact goal_id and revision. After session resume or fork, an active goal is disarmed: when a human asks to continue or resume in any wording or language, use update_goal action resume to rearm it. Mark complete only when the objective is actually achieved. Mark blocked only after the same blocking condition persists for at least 3 consecutive goal rounds, and report that concrete condition in blocked_reason; difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not blocked.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. A path without a file extension is accepted; the format is detected from the file content, so normalized attachment paths can be passed directly without copying or renaming. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: skill

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

tools.description: Update the exact current goal revision. edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. tner. This is a **Critical** priority item.

For example, if the term sheet specifies a general indemnification cap of 12.5% of enterprise value for a transaction with a \$200 million enterprise value, the SPA\'s general indemnification cap should be \$25,000,000. If the seller\'s draft sets the cap at \$20,000,000 (10% of enterprise value), the associate must flag this as a deviation from the term sheet and mark up the draft to reflect the agreed \$25,000,000 cap.

**R&W Insurance Considerations.** In transactions where the buyer is obtaining representations and warranties insurance (see Section 8), the indemnification cap may be subject to additional negotiation dynamics. The R&W insurer may require a certain retention level (the amount of loss the buyer must bear before the policy responds), which interacts with the SPA\'s basket/deductible and cap structure. However, the SPA cap itself must conform to the term sheet regardless of the R&W Insurance structure. The R&W Insurance policy supplements the seller\'s indemnification obligations --- it does not replace them, and the availability of insurance does not justify a reduction in the SPA cap below the term sheet level.

**Market Data.** In recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm, general indemnification caps have ranged from 10% to 15% of enterprise value. The 12.5% figure is squarely within the market range and represents the firm\'s standard recommendation for PE buyers in this sector. Caps below 10% of enterprise value are below market for environmental services acquisitions and should not be accepted without partner authorization. Caps at the higher end of the range (15%) may be appropriate for transactions with elevated environmental risk profiles.

**Escrow Mechanics.** The escrow amount (typically 7.5% of enterprise value --- see Section 5.4 for details) does NOT limit the buyer\'s right to recover under the indemnification provisions. For non-Fundamental Representation claims, the escrow is the first source of recovery, but the buyer\'s right to indemnification extends to the full amount of the general cap. Claims exceeding the escrow may be pursued directly against the seller (or, in the case of an equity rollover, may be offset against future payments) up to the general cap amount. The SPA must clearly and unambiguously state that the escrow does not constitute a limitation on the buyer\'s indemnification rights and that the buyer may pursue claims directly against the seller for amounts exceeding the escrow balance, up to the general indemnification cap. Any language in the seller\'s draft that could be interpreted as limiting the buyer\'s recovery to the escrow amount must be struck.

**[5.2 Basket / Deductible]{.underline}**

**Firm Standard.** A true deductible (not a tipping basket) of 0.75% to 1.0% of enterprise value is the market standard for middle-market transactions in the environmental services sector. Under a true deductible structure, the buyer bears the first dollar of indemnifiable losses up to the deductible amount; once the aggregate losses exceed the deductible, the buyer recovers only the excess over the deductible amount (not the full amount of losses from the first dollar). This is distinguished from a \"tipping basket\" (also called a \"threshold\" or \"first dollar\" basket), under which the basket functions as a threshold --- once aggregate losses exceed the basket amount, the buyer recovers the full amount of losses from the first dollar.

A 1% deductible is within the acceptable range and generally should not be marked up if it appears in the seller\'s draft. A deductible below 0.75% is better than market for the buyer and should obviously be accepted. A deductible above 1.25% should be pushed back as above-market.

**Carve-outs from the Basket.** The following categories of claims must be carved out of (i.e., not subject to) the basket. This is non-negotiable:

> \(a\) Claims for breach of Fundamental Representations;
>
> \(b\) Claims for fraud or willful misconduct;
>
> \(c\) Special Indemnities for known environmental liabilities (see Section 6); and
>
> \(d\) Claims for breach of Tax Representations (in many transactions).

Associates should confirm that these carve-outs are clearly stated in the SPA and that there is no ambiguity about their application.

**Mini-Basket.** Some seller drafts include a per-claim mini-basket (sometimes called a \"de minimis threshold\"), typically set at \$50,000 or \$100,000, below which individual claims are excluded from the calculation of aggregate losses for purposes of the basket. A mini-basket at a reasonable level is generally acceptable and serves the legitimate purpose of filtering out nuisance claims. A mini-basket above \$150,000 for a middle-market transaction in the \$100M--\$350M range should be resisted as disproportionate.

**[5.3 Sandbagging]{.underline}**

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** The SPA MUST contain an express pro-sandbagging provision. The firm\'s standard is that the buyer\'s right to indemnification under the agreement shall not be limited, diminished, or otherwise affected by any investigation, due diligence review, or knowledge obtained by or on behalf of the buyer before or after the closing, regardless of whether such knowledge was obtained before or after the execution of the agreement.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft contains an anti-sandbagging provision --- i.e., language providing that the buyer cannot recover for breaches of representations of which the buyer had \"Knowledge\" as of the closing date, or language providing that the buyer\'s indemnification rights are limited to the extent the buyer \"did not know\" of the breach prior to closing --- this language MUST be struck in its entirety and replaced with affirmative pro-sandbagging language. **Priority: CRITICAL.**

**Rationale.** In private equity acquisitions, the buyer conducts extensive due diligence through financial, legal, environmental, regulatory, and operational workstreams. Through this process, the buyer may become aware of potential representation breaches prior to closing --- for example, the environmental due diligence may reveal a potential CERCLA exposure that was not fully disclosed by the seller, or the legal due diligence may identify a non-compliance issue that arguably constitutes a breach of the environmental compliance representation.

An anti-sandbagging clause would penalize the buyer for conducting thorough due diligence by stripping the buyer of indemnification rights with respect to matters discovered during diligence. This creates a perverse incentive for the buyer to limit its own diligence, which is contrary to prudent deal practice and contrary to the interests of both parties (since thorough diligence benefits the transaction by identifying and addressing issues before closing).

More fundamentally, the buyer\'s right to rely on the seller\'s representations and warranties as a contractual allocation of risk is independent of what the buyer discovers during due diligence. The seller\'s representations serve as the seller\'s contractual commitment that certain facts are true and as the seller\'s assumption of the risk of indemnification if those facts prove to be untrue. This risk allocation is a core element of the purchase price negotiation --- the buyer is paying a price that reflects, among other things, the seller\'s representations about the state of the business. An anti-sandbagging clause would shift this risk allocation by relieving the seller of its indemnification obligation whenever the buyer independently discovers the breach, which fundamentally undermines the bargained-for indemnification structure.

**Delaware Law.** Delaware law does not impose a clear default rule on sandbagging. Unlike some jurisdictions that apply a common-law anti-sandbagging rule (under which a buyer\'s pre-closing knowledge of a breach may bar recovery), Delaware courts have not definitively adopted either a pro-sandbagging or anti-sandbagging default rule. This uncertainty makes contractual clarity essential. By including an express pro-sandbagging provision, the parties eliminate any ambiguity about the buyer\'s right to recover regardless of pre-closing knowledge.

**Sample Pro-Sandbagging Language:**

> *\"The right to indemnification or other remedy based on the representations, warranties, covenants, and obligations set forth in this Agreement shall not be affected by any investigation conducted by or on behalf of Buyer or any knowledge acquired (or capable of being acquired) by Buyer at any time, whether before or after the execution and delivery of this Agreement or the Closing Date, with respect to the accuracy or inaccuracy of, or compliance with, any such representation, warranty, covenant, or obligation. No claim for indemnification under this Article \[\_\_\] shall be defeated or diminished by reason of any investigation, knowledge, or notice of Buyer, whether before or after the date hereof, and regardless of whether such investigation, knowledge, or notice was available to or obtained by Buyer prior to or after the Closing.\"*

**[5.4 Escrow Mechanics]{.underline}**

**Escrow Amount.** The standard escrow amount for environmental services acquisitions is 7.5% to 10% of enterprise value. The escrow agent should be an independent trust company with experience in M&A escrow administration (e.g., Pinnacle Trust Company, N.A. or a similar institutional fiduciary). The escrow agent should not be an affiliate of either party or of the buyer\'s lender.

**Escrow Release Schedule.** The escrow release schedule should be structured as follows:

> \(a\) **General Claims Escrow.** Released eighteen (18) months post-closing (corresponding to the low end of the general representation survival period), less any amounts reserved for pending and unresolved claims as of the release date.
>
> \(b\) **Fundamental Representations and Special Indemnity Escrow.** Released thirty-six (36) months post-closing, less any amounts reserved for pending and unresolved claims as of the release date. This extended hold period corresponds to the minimum environmental representation survival period and the extended escrow for Special Indemnity claims.

**Escrow Does Not Limit Recovery.** As noted in Section 5.1, the escrow does not limit the buyer\'s indemnification rights. It is a source of funds for the buyer\'s convenience and security, not a cap on recovery. The SPA must clearly state this principle, and the escrow agreement must be consistent with it.

**Escrow Agreement.** The escrow agreement should be negotiated simultaneously with the SPA and should be attached as an exhibit to the SPA (or, at minimum, the material terms of the escrow agreement should be set forth in the SPA itself). The escrow agreement should provide for joint instructions for releases, a dispute resolution mechanism (typically requiring a final, non-appealable court order or arbitration award for disputed claims), and reasonable investment parameters for the escrowed funds.

**[Section 6: Special Indemnities for Known Environmental Liabilities]{.underline}**

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** Where due diligence has identified a specific, known environmental liability --- such as a pending or threatened CERCLA claim, an EPA information request under CERCLA Section 104(e), a state environmental enforcement action, an ongoing remediation obligation, or any other identified environmental matter --- and the estimated potential liability is \$1,000,000 or more, the SPA MUST include a \"Special Indemnity\" provision for that specific liability.

The Special Indemnity is a distinct indemnification mechanism that operates separately from and in addition to the general representation and warranty indemnification. Its parameters are as follows:

**Survival.** The Special Indemnity must survive for seventy-two (72) months (six years) post-closing. This extended survival period reflects the long-tail nature of CERCLA and environmental enforcement actions, which --- as discussed in Section 4.2 --- often take years to progress from initial inquiry to resolution. A seventy-two month survival period provides the buyer with a meaningful window within which to assert claims as the environmental matter develops and the buyer\'s actual losses become ascertainable.

**Not Subject to the Basket/Deductible.** The Special Indemnity is a dollar-one indemnification obligation. It is not subject to the general deductible described in Section 5.2. The rationale is straightforward: the basket/deductible is designed to filter out immaterial or de minimis claims arising from general representation breaches. A known environmental liability with an estimated exposure of \$1,000,000 or more is, by definition, not immaterial --- it is a specifically identified risk that has been factored into the purchase price negotiation and that requires dedicated indemnification protection.

**Not Subject to the General Cap.** The Special Indemnity is not counted toward the general indemnification cap described in Section 5.1. It operates as a separate, independent indemnification obligation with its own limitations. The Special Indemnity may be subject to its own sub-cap, which is negotiated on a matter-specific basis and typically reflects the high end of the estimated liability range identified in the environmental due diligence. For example, if the estimated liability range for a CERCLA exposure is \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, the Special Indemnity sub-cap might be negotiated at \$6,000,000 or \$7,500,000 (the high end of the range plus a reasonable buffer).

**Escrow.** Escrow funds designated for the Special Indemnity should be held for thirty-six (36) months post-closing, consistent with the extended escrow for Fundamental Representations described in Section 5.4. After thirty-six months, the buyer may still assert Special Indemnity claims (through the seventy-two month survival period), but recovery would be sought directly from the seller rather than from escrow.

**Specific Identification.** The Special Indemnity provision must specifically identify the environmental matter by name, site location, applicable regulatory proceeding number (if any), nature of the liability (e.g., \"CERCLA response cost liability arising from historical disposal at \[Site Name\]\"), and the specific representation or due diligence finding that identified the matter. The identified matters should be listed on a dedicated schedule to the SPA (typically a \"Schedule of Scheduled Environmental Matters\" or similar title).

**Rationale.** Known environmental liabilities are not appropriately covered by general representation and warranty indemnification for several reasons:

> \(i\) Known environmental matters are already disclosed (and, in many cases, scheduled as exceptions to the environmental representations). Because they are disclosed, they may not technically constitute \"breaches\" of the representations in the traditional sense, potentially leaving the buyer without a general indemnification claim.
>
> \(ii\) General survival periods (whether eighteen months for general representations or even thirty-six months for environmental representations) are inadequate for the long-tail nature of many environmental enforcement actions, which may take five to ten years to resolve.
>
> \(iii\) The basket/deductible could prevent recovery for environmental matters falling within the lower end of the estimated liability range, particularly where the buyer has other general indemnification claims consuming the deductible.
>
> \(iv\) The general indemnification cap may be consumed by other claims, leaving the buyer unprotected for the specific known liability that was the subject of purchase price negotiation.

**Specific Instruction.** If environmental due diligence has identified a known CERCLA exposure --- such as a pending EPA information request at a specific disposal facility --- with an estimated liability range of \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, the associate MUST ensure that the SPA contains a Special Indemnity provision specifically covering that exposure. If the seller\'s draft SPA fails to include such a provision, the associate should draft and insert a Special Indemnity provision and raise it with the seller\'s counsel as a required addition. Do not treat the absence of a Special Indemnity as a minor markup item; it is a **Critical** priority item that must be escalated to the responsible partner if the seller resists.

**Sample Special Indemnity Language:**

> *\"(a) From and after the Closing, Seller shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Buyer and its Affiliates (including, after the Closing, the Company) and their respective officers, directors, employees, agents, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \'Buyer Indemnified Parties\') from and against any and all Losses arising out of, resulting from, or relating to the Scheduled Environmental Matters set forth on Schedule 6.1 (the \'Special Environmental Indemnity\').*
>
> *\"(b) The Special Environmental Indemnity shall survive the Closing for a period of seventy-two (72) months following the Closing Date, and any claim for indemnification under this Section \[\_\_\] must be asserted by written notice delivered to Seller on or prior to the date that is seventy-two (72) months following the Closing Date.*
>
> *\"(c) The Special Environmental Indemnity shall not be subject to the Deductible set forth in Section \[\_\_\] or the Cap set forth in Section \[\_\_\]. The maximum aggregate liability of Seller under this Section \[\_\_\] with respect to each Scheduled Environmental Matter shall be the amount set forth opposite such Scheduled Environmental Matter on Schedule 6.1 (each, a \'Special Indemnity Sub-Cap\').*
>
> *\"(d) For the avoidance of doubt, Losses recovered by Buyer Indemnified Parties pursuant to this Section \[\_\_\] shall not reduce or otherwise affect the Cap available for claims under Section \[\_\_\].\"*

**[Section 7: Earnout Provisions]{.underline}**

**[7.1 General Guidance on Earnouts]{.underline}**

Earnout provisions in PE acquisitions are generally disfavored by the firm\'s PE buyer clients because they create ongoing economic entanglements with the seller, generate disputes over post-closing operations, and restrict the buyer\'s ability to integrate and restructure the acquired business. However, earnouts are sometimes commercially necessary to bridge a valuation gap between the buyer\'s and seller\'s expectations of the target\'s future performance. When an earnout is commercially required, it must be structured carefully to preserve the buyer\'s operational flexibility post-closing.

The key structural elements of any earnout provision are:

> \(a\) **Clearly defined earn-out metric.** The earn-out metric should be specifically defined --- typically Adjusted EBITDA --- with all adjustments, add-backs, and exclusions set forth in the SPA or in an exhibit to the SPA. Ambiguous metrics are a leading source of post-closing disputes.
>
> \(b\) **Measurement period.** The measurement period (typically twelve to twenty-four months post-closing) must be clearly specified, including the start date and end date.
>
> \(c\) **Payment mechanics.** The timing, manner, and conditions of payment should be specified, including the buyer\'s obligation to deliver a calculation statement, the seller\'s right to review and dispute the calculation, and the deadline for payment.
>
> \(d\) **Dispute resolution.** Disputes over the earn-out calculation should be resolved by an independent accounting firm, with the costs allocated between the parties based on the outcome.
>
> \(e\) **Operational covenants.** The scope and nature of any covenants regarding the buyer\'s post-closing conduct of the business during the earnout period. This is addressed in detail in Section 7.2 below.

**[7.2 Buyer\'s Operational Covenants During Earnout Period]{.underline}**

**THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** Earnout provisions MUST NOT contain any affirmative operational covenant requiring the buyer to operate the acquired business \"in a manner consistent with past practice,\" \"in a manner designed to maximize the Earnout Payment,\" \"in substantially the same manner as operated prior to the Closing,\" or similar language that would restrict the buyer\'s ability to integrate, restructure, make capital investments, change pricing strategies, adjust compensation structures, enter new markets, exit underperforming lines of business, or otherwise operate the acquired business as the buyer sees fit in its sole discretion.

**Acceptable Standard.** The only covenant the firm will accept regarding the buyer\'s post-closing conduct in relation to an earnout is a narrow negative covenant providing that the buyer will not take any action with the **primary purpose** of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. This carefully calibrated formulation achieves the appropriate balance of interests:

> \(a\) It protects the seller against bad-faith manipulation of the earn-out metric --- for example, the buyer cannot artificially depress EBITDA by diverting revenue to other portfolio companies or by loading excessive corporate allocations onto the target solely to reduce the earnout payment;
>
> \(b\) It preserves the buyer\'s full operational flexibility to manage the acquired business in accordance with the buyer\'s investment thesis, business judgment, and strategic objectives; and
>
> \(c\) It is consistent with the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing under Delaware law, which courts have applied to earnout provisions even in the absence of an express covenant, but which does not impose an obligation to maximize the earnout.

**Rationale.** A PE buyer acquires a platform business precisely to implement operational improvements, achieve synergies, execute strategic initiatives, and drive value creation. An earnout covenant requiring \"past practice\" operations or requiring the buyer to \"maximize\" the earnout payment would effectively handcuff the buyer for the entire earnout period --- potentially twelve to twenty-four months --- undermining the very investment thesis that motivated the acquisition. Moreover, courts have enforced restrictive earnout covenants as written, even where the covenant\'s practical effect was to prevent the buyer from making value-enhancing changes. See, e.g., decisions of the Delaware Court of Chancery interpreting express earnout covenants according to their terms. Precise drafting is therefore essential to avoid unintended restrictions on the buyer\'s post-closing operations.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft includes language requiring the buyer to operate the business \"in a manner consistent with past practice and in good faith to maximize the Earnout Payment,\" or similar language imposing affirmative operational obligations, this MUST be struck and replaced with the narrow \"primary purpose\" negative covenant. The associate should provide a margin comment explaining the firm\'s position and the rationale for the change. **Priority: HIGH.**

**Sample Acceptable Earnout Covenant Language:**

> *\"Following the Closing, Buyer shall not, and shall cause the Company not to, take any action with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this Section \[\_\_\] shall restrict Buyer\'s right to operate, integrate, restructure, or otherwise manage the Company and its business in Buyer\'s sole discretion, including without limitation the right to make capital expenditure decisions, pricing changes, personnel decisions, strategic investments, acquisitions, dispositions, organizational restructurings, and operational modifications, and no such action shall constitute a breach of this Section \[\_\_\] unless taken with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment.\"*

**Definition of Adjusted EBITDA for Earnout Purposes.** The definition of Adjusted EBITDA used for the earnout calculation should be precisely defined in the SPA and should include add-backs for the following categories of items to prevent manipulation claims in either direction:

> \(a\) Buyer-directed integration costs and restructuring charges;
>
> \(b\) Transaction-related expenses (including legal, accounting, and advisory fees related to the acquisition);
>
> \(c\) Non-recurring items, including one-time litigation costs, regulatory penalties, and extraordinary items;
>
> \(d\) Corporate overhead allocations from the buyer or the buyer\'s other portfolio companies (to the extent not charged to the target on a consistent basis prior to the closing); and
>
> \(e\) Intercompany charges from the buyer o requirements for non-compete agreements. Some jurisdictions (most notably California) are hostile to non-compete covenants generally, although the sale-of-business exception may apply. Associates should identify the governing law of the non-compete provision and confirm that the covenant\'s terms are consistent with the requirements of that jurisdiction. Overbroad covenants risk being voided entirely rather than judicially reformed, depending on the jurisdiction\'s approach to reformation (sometimes called \"blue penciling\").

**Non-Solicitation.** In addition to the non-compete, the SPA should include non-solicitation covenants prohibiting the seller and its principals from (a) soliciting or hiring employees of the target and (b) soliciting or diverting customers or suppliers of the target. The non-solicitation period should match the non-compete period.

**[Section 11: Knowledge Qualifiers and Other Definitional Issues]{.underline}**

**[11.1 Knowledge Definition]{.underline}**

The definition of \"Knowledge\" (or \"to the knowledge of the Seller/Company\") is used throughout the SPA to qualify certain representations and warranties. The scope of the Knowledge definition determines whether the seller\'s representations are based solely on the actual awareness of specified individuals or whether they extend to information that such individuals should have known after making reasonable inquiry.

**Firm Standard.** For targets with fewer than 500 employees (which includes the majority of environmental services targets in the middle-market range), actual knowledge of the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer (or their functional equivalents) is an acceptable Knowledge standard. These individuals typically have sufficient familiarity with the target\'s operations, financial condition, regulatory compliance status, and material contracts to provide meaningful knowledge-qualified representations.

For targets with more than 500 employees, or for targets with geographically dispersed operations where the CEO and CFO may not have direct visibility into all material matters, a constructive knowledge standard --- knowledge after reasonable inquiry --- applied to a broader group of specified individuals (including, for example, the VP of Operations, the VP of Environmental Compliance, and regional managers) is preferred.

**Note to Associates.** Some associates reflexively mark up knowledge definitions to add constructive knowledge or to expand the list of knowledge individuals in every transaction. For smaller targets where actual knowledge of the CEO and CFO is the standard, this markup is unnecessary and can create unproductive negotiations. Focus your markup efforts on higher-priority items identified in this playbook.

**[11.2 Acceptable Provisions --- When Not to Mark Up]{.underline}**

This section provides guidance on provisions that, while potentially appearing sub-optimal from the buyer\'s perspective, are within acceptable market ranges and should generally NOT be marked up in the seller\'s draft. Disciplined markup is essential to maintaining the credibility of the associate, the responsible partner, and the firm. Marking up provisions that are squarely within market range wastes negotiating capital, creates unnecessary friction, and signals to the seller\'s counsel that the buyer\'s team is either inexperienced or unreasonable.

The following provisions are within the firm\'s acceptable range and should not be marked up absent deal-specific partner instructions to the contrary:

> **Basket/Deductible at 0.75%--1.0% of Enterprise Value.** As discussed in Section 5.2, this is within the firm\'s acceptable range for middle-market environmental services transactions. A basket at 1.0% of enterprise value should not be marked up. Do not attempt to negotiate the basket down to 0.5% or lower merely because a lower basket would be better for the buyer --- the improvement is marginal and the negotiating capital is better spent elsewhere.
>
> **Knowledge Qualifier Limited to Actual Knowledge of CEO and CFO for Targets Under 500 Employees.** As discussed in Section 11.1, this is the firm\'s accepted standard for smaller targets. Do not mark up the knowledge definition to add constructive knowledge or additional knowledge individuals unless the target has more than 500 employees or the responsible partner instructs otherwise.
>
> **Good Standing Certificates Dated Within 5--10 Business Days of Closing.** This is the standard timeframe for good standing certificates in M&A transactions. Secretary of state offices in most jurisdictions will issue certificates within this timeframe. Do not mark up a 10-business-day requirement to demand same-day certificates or certificates dated within 3 business days, as this creates logistical complications without meaningful benefit.
>
> **Delaware Governing Law.** Delaware is the preferred governing law for SPAs in transactions where both the buyer and the seller have connections to Delaware (e.g., where one or both parties are Delaware entities). Delaware\'s well-developed body of corporate and contract law, sophisticated judiciary, and predictable outcomes make it an optimal choice. Do not mark up a Delaware governing law clause to substitute another jurisdiction\'s law absent specific instructions from the responsible partner.

**General Principle.** The associate\'s credibility --- and the firm\'s reputation --- depends on disciplined, strategic markup. Do not mark up provisions that are within market range merely to demonstrate thoroughness or to generate a longer redline. Focus markup energy exclusively on provisions that (i) deviate from the executed term sheet, (ii) violate the requirements set forth in this playbook, or (iii) expose the buyer to material uncompensated risk. Every markup should be defensible with reference to the term sheet, this playbook, or a specific risk identified in due diligence.

**[Section 12: Environmental Regulatory Considerations (Sector-Specific)]{.underline}**

**[12.1 Environmental Permit Transfers]{.underline}**

In a stock acquisition, the target entity itself does not change --- the same legal entity that held the environmental permits before the transaction continues to hold them after the transaction. This is one of the principal advantages of a stock purchase structure for environmental services targets with complex permitting portfolios. However, the mere fact that the permit-holding entity does not change does not mean that the change of control is transparent to regulators.

Many state environmental regulatory programs --- including programs authorized under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, and the Clean Water Act --- require notification to, or approval from, the issuing regulatory agency upon a change of control of the permit holder, even in stock purchase transactions. The specific requirements vary by state and by permit type, and failure to comply with applicable notification or approval requirements can result in permit violations, enforcement actions, or, in extreme cases, permit revocation.

**States of Particular Note.** Based on the firm\'s recent transaction experience in the environmental services sector, the following states impose change-of-control notification or approval requirements that are particularly relevant:

> \(a\) **Oregon:** The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"DEQ\") requires change-of-ownership notifications for certain categories of environmental permits, including RCRA hazardous waste facility permits and water quality permits.
>
> \(b\) **Washington:** The Washington Department of Ecology requires similar notifications and, in some cases, formal approval for changes of ownership affecting certain environmental permits.
>
> \(c\) **California:** The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (\"DTSC\") has specific requirements for notification and, in certain circumstances, prior approval of changes of control for hazardous waste facility permits.
>
> \(d\) **Nevada:** The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (\"NDEP\") imposes change-of-ownership notification requirements for certain permits.

**Firm Standard.** The SPA should include both (a) a representation regarding the current status of all Environmental Permits held by the target (including confirmation that all permits are in full force and effect, that no permit is subject to pending revocation or suspension, and that no conditions exist that could give rise to revocation or suspension) AND (b) pre-closing and post-closing covenants requiring the seller\'s cooperation in the notification, transfer, or re-issuance of Environmental Permits as required by applicable law. The cooperation covenant should extend through a period of at least twelve (12) months post-closing to cover permits with longer regulatory processing timelines.

Associates should review the environmental due diligence memo for a comprehensive list of all target permits and should flag any permits that require transfer notifications or regulatory approvals in connection with the change of control.

**[12.2 Government Contract Considerations]{.underline}**

Environmental services companies frequently derive a significant portion of their revenue from government contracts --- including federal, state, and local contracts --- for environmental remediation, environmental consulting, environmental monitoring, and related services. Government contracts present unique legal issues in the acquisition context that associates must address in the SPA.

**Federal Government Contracts.** Federal government contracts are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act (41 U.S.C. § 6305), which generally prohibits the assignment of government contracts without the consent of the contracting officer. In addition, FAR 42.12 sets forth the procedures for novation agreements when a contractor undergoes a change of ownership. A novation agreement is a three-party agreement among the government, the original contractor, and the successor contractor, pursuant to which the government recognizes the successor as the contractor under the existing contract.

Even in stock purchase transactions --- where the contracting entity does not change --- certain changes in ownership may trigger novation or recognition requirements under FAR. Specifically, FAR 42.1204 provides that a novation agreement may be required when a contractor is acquired by another entity, even if the contractor entity continues to exist. The determination of whether a novation is required depends on the circumstances, including whether the contractor entity remains intact and continues to perform under the contract.

**Firm Standard.** The SPA should include:

> \(i\) A representation regarding the status of all government contracts held by the target, including confirmation that all contracts are in good standing, that no contracts are subject to pending termination for default or convenience, and that no debarment or suspension proceedings are pending or threatened;
>
> \(ii\) A pre-closing covenant requiring the seller and the target to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain novation or recognition agreements from applicable government contracting officers, to the extent required by applicable law or regulation; and
>
> \(iii\) Consideration of whether government contract consent should be a closing condition. For targets where government contracts represent a material portion of revenue (typically more than 20%), the failure to obtain required novation agreements may justify a closing condition. For targets with a smaller government contract exposure, a pre-closing covenant with commercially reasonable efforts may be sufficient.

Associates should cross-reference the government contracts section of the due diligence memo and consult with the firm\'s Government Contracts Practice Group for guidance on specific novation requirements.

**[Section 13: Closing Conditions]{.underline}**

**[13.1 Standard Buyer Closing Conditions]{.underline}**

The SPA must include the following standard closing conditions for the buyer\'s benefit. These conditions are required in every PE acquisition SPA and should not be omitted or materially diluted:

> \(a\) **Accuracy of Representations and Warranties.** The seller\'s representations and warranties must be true and correct as of the closing date as though made on such date (with appropriate exceptions for representations made as of a specific date). For non-Fundamental Representations, accuracy is qualified by a Material Adverse Effect standard (i.e., the representations must be true and correct except where the failure to be true and correct would not, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect). For Fundamental Representations, accuracy must be true and correct in all respects (other than de minimis inaccuracies).
>
> \(b\) **Compliance with Covenants.** The seller and the target must have complied in all material respects with all covenants and agreements required to be performed by them at or prior to the closing.
>
> \(c\) **No Material Adverse Effect.** No Material Adverse Effect shall have occurred since the date of the agreement.
>
> \(d\) **HSR Act Clearance.** If the transaction is reportable under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, all applicable waiting periods shall have expired or been terminated.
>
> \(e\) **Third-Party Consents.** All consents required for the assignment or transfer of material contracts (including material customer contracts, material supplier contracts, and material leases) shall have been obtained.
>
> \(f\) **Delivery of Payoff Letters.** Payoff letters from all holders of target indebtedness shall have been delivered in accordance with the SPA\'s requirements (see Section 9.2).
>
> \(g\) **Officer\'s Certificate.** An officer of the seller or the target shall have delivered a certificate certifying the satisfaction of the conditions set forth in clauses (a) through (c) above.
>
> \(h\) **Secretary\'s Certificate.** The secretary (or equivalent officer) of the target shall have delivered a certificate attaching the target\'s organizational documents, resolutions authorizing the transaction, and incumbency of officers.
>
> \(i\) **Good Standing Certificates.** Good standing certificates (or certificates of existence, as applicable) for the target from its jurisdiction of organization and each jurisdiction in which it is qualified to do business, dated within ten (10) business days of the closing date.
>
> \(j\) **Employment and Non-Compete Agreements.** Executed employment agreements and/or non-competition agreements with key employees identified in the SPA or the term sheet.
>
> \(k\) **FIRPTA Certificate.** A certificate from the seller meeting the requirements of Treasury Regulations Section 1.1445-2(b)(2), certifying that the seller is not a foreign person for purposes of FIRPTA.
>
> \(l\) **R&W Insurance Policy.** If the buyer is obtaining R&W Insurance, evidence that the R&W Insurance policy has been bound and is in full force and effect.
>
> \(m\) **No Injunctions.** No temporary restraining order, preliminary or permanent injunction, or other order or decree issued by any court of competent jurisdiction or governmental authority shall be in effect that prevents or prohibits the consummation of the transactions contemplated by the agreement.

**[13.2 Sector-Specific Closing Conditions]{.underline}**

In addition to the standard closing conditions set forth in Section 13.1, the following sector-specific closing conditions should be included in environmental services acquisitions where applicable:

> \(a\) **Government Contract Novation or Recognition.** Where the target holds material government contracts that require novation or recognition agreements in connection with the change of control, the receipt of such novation or recognition agreements (or, at minimum, written confirmation from the applicable contracting officer that the novation process is underway and that interim performance will be permitted) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.2 for further guidance.
>
> \(b\) **Environmental Permit Transfer Notifications.** Where applicable state law requires notification to or approval from a regulatory agency in connection with a change of control of the permit holder, confirmation that all required notifications have been filed (and, where prior approval is required, that such approval has been obtained) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.1 for further guidance.
>
> \(c\) **No New Environmental Claims.** Confirmation that no new material environmental claim, enforcement action, notice of violation, CERCLA information request, or similar regulatory action has been received by the target since the date of the agreement that would, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect.
>
> \(d\) **Environmental Impairment Liability Insurance.** Confirmation that all environmental impairment liability insurance policies maintained by the target remain in full force and effect as of the closing date, with coverage levels no less than those in effect as of the date of the agreement.

**[Section 14: Checklist Summary --- Key Markup Items for Environmental Services SPAs]{.underline}**

The following checklist summarizes all critical and high-priority items covered in this playbook. Associates should use this checklist as a quick-reference guide when performing markup of a seller\'s draft SPA in an environmental services transaction. Each item includes a priority designation and a cross-reference to the relevant section of this playbook for detailed guidance.

1\. **MAE Definition --- Disproportionate Impact Qualifier** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that all industry-specific and regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition include a \"disproportionate impact\" qualifier. If the carve-out for \"changes in the environmental services industry generally\" or \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" lacks the qualifier, flag and correct immediately. *(Ref. Section 2.1)*

2\. **Interim Covenants --- Affiliate Transaction Restriction** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the interim operating covenants include a specific restriction prohibiting the target from entering into, amending, extending, or terminating any affiliate transaction without buyer\'s prior written consent. *(Ref. Section 3.2)*

3\. **Indemnification Cap --- Conformity with Term Sheet** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that the general indemnification cap matches the percentage agreed in the executed term sheet (typical range: 10%--15% of enterprise value; firm standard: 12.5%). Flag and correct any deviation from the term sheet. *(Ref. Section 5.1)*

4\. **Environmental Representation Survival --- Minimum 36 Months** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that environmental representations survive for a minimum of 36 months post-closing, carved out from the general representation survival period. Preferred position: full statute of limitations. *(Ref. Section 4.2)*

5\. **Pro-Sandbagging Clause** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that the SPA contains an affirmative pro-sandbagging provision. If the seller\'s draft contains an anti-sandbagging clause, strike it and replace with pro-sandbagging language. *(Ref. Section 5.3)*

6\. **Special Indemnity for Known Environmental Liabilities** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that a Special Indemnity is included for each identified environmental liability with estimated exposure of \$1,000,000 or more; 72-month survival; dollar-one recovery (outside the basket); not subject to the general cap. *(Ref. Section 6)*

7\. **Earnout Operational Covenants --- No Affirmative Obligations** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that earnout provisions do not contain affirmative operational covenants (e.g., \"operate in a manner consistent with past practice\" or \"maximize the Earnout Payment\"). Only the narrow \"primary purpose\" negative covenant is acceptable. *(Ref. Section 7.2)*

8\. **R&W Insurance Subrogation Waiver** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA includes a waiver of the R&W insurer\'s subrogation rights against the seller (except for fraud). *(Ref. Section 8.2)*

9\. **Payoff Letters as Closing Condition** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA requires delivery of payoff letters from all holders of target indebtedness at least 3 business days prior to closing, and that delivery is a condition to buyer\'s obligation to close. *(Ref. Section 9.2)*

10\. **Non-Compete Scope** \[MEDIUM-HIGH\]. Confirm that non-compete provisions match the term sheet in duration, geographic scope, and business scope. Avoid overbroad restrictions that could capture seller\'s unrelated business activities or that risk unenforceability. *(Ref. Section 10.1)*

11\. **Government Contract Novation** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA addresses Anti-Assignment Act and FAR novation requirements, including representations, pre-closing covenants, and (where applicable) closing conditions for material government contracts. *(Ref. Section 12.2)*

12\. **Environmental Permit Transfer Covenants** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA includes cooperation covenants for environmental permit notifications and transfers required by applicable state law in connection with the change of control. *(Ref. Section 12.1)*

13\. **Do Not Mark Up** \[GUIDANCE\]. The following items are within acceptable market range and should generally not be marked up: basket/deductible at 0.75%--1.0% of enterprise value; actual knowledge of CEO and CFO for targets with fewer than 500 employees; good standing certificates dated within 5--10 business days of closing; Delaware governing law. *(Ref. Section 11.2)*

**[I. Executive Summary]{.underline}**

Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP\'s Environmental Practice Group has completed its environmental due diligence review of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. (\"Cascadia\" or the \"Company\"), an Oregon corporation headquartered at 8700 SW Tualatin-Sherwood Road, Suite 200, Tualatin, Oregon 97062. (\"Seller\" or \"Evergreen\"), at a base enterprise value of \$215,000,000. This acquisition will serve as a platform investment for Whitmore Capital Partners LLC Fund III.

Our environmental due diligence review has identified four principal areas of environmental concern that the deal team must address in the Stock Purchase Agreement:

1\. **Dalton Creek CERCLA Exposure (HIGH RISK).** The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has issued an information request under CERCLA § 104(e) to Cascadia regarding the Company\'s former operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility. We estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in the range of \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, depending upon EPA\'s cost allocation approach and the solvency of other potentially responsible parties.

2\. **Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia is actively performing environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site in Milwaukie, Oregon, under contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. This exposure is a contractual obligation and is covered by a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy with a \$10,000,000 policy limit, which appears adequate.

3\. **Environmental Permit Portfolio (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia holds 23 active environmental permits across four states. Although the transaction is structured as a stock purchase, multiple state environmental regulatory programs require notification to or approval from the issuing agency upon a change in control of the permit holder. Failure to obtain required novations could result in contract termination, eliminating a material revenue stream.

This memorandum provides detailed findings for each of these areas and sets forth **specific recommendations for SPA provisions** that the deal team should incorporate into its markup of the Seller\'s draft agreement. These recommendations are informed by the executed term sheet dated September 10, 2025, applicable federal and state environmental law, and industry practice for acquisitions in the environmental services sector.
